Macedonian mouse neonates are born after a relatively prolonged gestation period for a small murid, with captive studies indicating that pregnancy lasts approximately 24 days [tg = approximately 24 days] when females are maintained at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. At birth, the altricial pups are exceptionally small, with a neonatal wet weight of only about 1 gram [Wwb = about 1 gram], a value that aligns closely with estimates derived from the closely related house mouse, Mus musculus. This diminutive birth mass is typical of muroid rodents that produce relatively large litters and invest heavily in postnatal lactation rather than prolonged gestation. The high degree of altriciality at parturition means that the offspring are highly dependent on maternal care for thermoregulation and nutrition during the initial days following the birth event.

By the time the pups reach 26 days after birth [tx = 26 days after birth], they are typically weaned and transition to a diet of solid food, a developmental milestone that is also observed under the standard thermal regime of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This age at weaning marks the cessation of the lactational dependency phase, during which the suckling juveniles have undergone rapid somatic growth fueled entirely by maternal milk. In the wild, the timing of this weaning event is critical, as it coincides with the seasonal availability of seeds and invertebrates that form the bulk of the adult diet. Post-weaning, the young individuals enter a juvenile stage characterized by continued mass gain and behavioral development before they approach reproductive maturity.

The species exhibits a life history strategy that is paced by a relatively fast tempo, with the maximum recorded lifespan being approximately 2.8 years [am = approximately 2.8 years] for individuals maintained at a physiological temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a figure derived from captive observations of the congener Mus musculoides. This longevity is modest compared to many other small mammals, reflecting a high-risk, high-fecundity life history typical of murine rodents. Respirometry trials on adults at the same physiological temperature have measured a maximum basal metabolic rate of 19.38 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 19.38 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. In natural populations, mortality rates are likely much higher due to predation and environmental stochasticity, meaning that relatively few individuals reach this senescent stage. Physiological death in older individuals is often preceded by a gradual decline in body condition and reproductive output, culminating in a failure to meet daily metabolic costs.

Female Macedonian mice attain a maximum adult body mass of approximately 15 grams [Wwi = approximately 15 grams], although field-captured individuals often range between 11 and 30 grams depending on habitat quality and seasonal food abundance. This ultimate body weight is attained after the completion of the juvenile growth phase and is typically reached by the time the female begins her first reproductive efforts. The species shows a clear pattern of sexual size dimorphism, with females generally being slightly heavier than males, a trait linked to the energetic demands of gestation and lactation. Measurements taken from museum specimen series confirm that this asymptotic mass is sustained throughout the breeding adult phase, after which body condition may deteriorate with advancing age.

The onset of reproductive activity in the Macedonian mouse is remarkably rapid, with sexual maturity in captive-reared individuals occurring at a mere 60 days since birth [tp = 60 days since birth] when housed at a constant 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Once reproductively active, fecundity is high: each litter typically contains 4.5 pups [N_R_i = each litter typically contains 4.5 pups], and females are capable of producing up to 4 litters each year [F_R_i = up to 4 litters each year], although this frequency is contingent on sustained food availability and a stable thermal environment. The maximum reproductive rate that results from this combination of litter size and annual litter frequency underscores the species' capacity for rapid population growth. In the field, females often breed synchronously during favorable seasons, producing a pulse of newborn offspring that quickly recruit into the breeding population.
